title: Stored biological specimen enables exposure of highly sensitive subject attributes
description: Sending a physical sample into long-term freezer storage creates a persistent repository of biological material. The specimen itself can reveal sensitive health, genetic, or physiological characteristics if accessed or analyzed beyond the originally expected purpose, so the storage flow introduces a privacy threat of information disclosure tied to biological-sample collection and retention.
assumptions: The stored sample remains linkable, directly or indirectly, to an individual participant and may be available for later testing or access.

title: Freezer storage of biological sample creates a durable identifiable presence of the data subject
description: A preserved biological sample is an enduring physical representation of the data subject. By placing the specimen into storage, the organization maintains data about the subject in a form that may persist for long periods, increasing the risk that others can detect the subject's participation or existence in the repository even without direct content access.
assumptions: Presence of a sample in storage can itself be privacy-relevant, for example because storage metadata, labels, or inventory records indicate that a person contributed a specimen.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort mapping: PANOPTIC PA03.11 clearly applies, but the exact LINDDUN detectability tree-node selection for physical specimen presence is approximate.

title: Stored specimen can support later re-identification or linkage to the participant
description: Once the physical sample is stored, it can potentially be re-associated with the participant through labels, freezer inventory references, chain-of-custody records, or intrinsic biological uniqueness. This creates a linkability/re-identification threat because the sample may be correlated with other records or identities over time.
assumptions: The sample is labeled, coded, or otherwise accompanied by operational metadata, or the biological material itself is sufficiently unique to support re-identification when combined with other datasets.
uncertainty_note: PA05.01.01 is not a perfect semantic match for the storage act itself, but it is relevant to the realistic downstream privacy risk created by storing identifiable biological material.

title: Returned de-identified sample ID may still permit re-identification
description: The LIMS sends sample metadata containing a de-identified ID back to the wet lab for use with the sample. If that identifier is only pseudonymous or remains linkable to other records available to the wet lab or nearby systems, the data may be insufficiently de-identified, enabling the subject behind the sample to be singled out or re-identified.
assumptions: Assumes the wet lab can access, infer, or later obtain auxiliary information or mappings that make the de-identified ID linkable to an individual or source sample.

title: De-identified identifier may fail to meet expected de-identification requirements
description: Because this flow distributes a de-identified ID for operational use, there is a risk that the masking or transformation applied in the LIMS is not strong enough for the wet-lab context. This can create non-compliance with data-minimization or de-identification obligations if the identifier remains reasonably attributable to a person or specimen donor.
assumptions: Assumes applicable policy, contractual, or regulatory requirements expect stronger de-identification for identifiers shared back to the wet lab.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected as a best-effort fit because PANOPTIC grounding is stronger than the exact LINDDUN Pro node mapping here.

title: Persistent storage of raw sequence data enables disclosure of highly sensitive genomic information
description: The flow stores digital raw sequence data in the cluster filesystem. Genomic sequence data is intrinsically sensitive and can reveal health traits, ancestry, and familial relationships. Persistently recording it in a shared storage system increases the opportunity for unauthorized disclosure if access controls, isolation, or retention controls are weak.
assumptions: The cluster filesystem is used for persistent storage accessible beyond the immediate sequencing instrument/workstation context, and the raw sequence data remains identifiable or highly linkable to an individual or sample.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 'Recording' is a best-fit PANOPTIC action for this storage event, but PANOPTIC retrieval may not include a more storage-specific sub-activity.

title: Raw sequence data may be stored without sufficient de-identification
description: If the sequence data is stored in raw form with direct identifiers, sample identifiers, or quasi-identifiers that can readily be linked back to a person, the filesystem becomes a point where data is insufficiently de-identified. This creates a risk that individuals can be singled out or their genomic data exposed beyond what is necessary for the storage purpose.
assumptions: The stored data may contain direct sample/patient identifiers in filenames, metadata, directory structure, or accompanying manifests, or the genomic data itself is treated as linkable personal data.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the stored sequence data or associated metadata has not been robustly de-identified/pseudonymized; if the environment already enforces strong separation of identifiers, this threat may be reduced.

title: Stored genomic data may be re-identified or linked back to a data subject
description: Even if some identifiers are removed before storage, raw genomic sequence data is often inherently identifying or can be re-associated with a person when combined with other datasets, manifests, or research records. Storing the data in the cluster filesystem creates a durable target for later re-identification and linkage attacks.
assumptions: Attackers or unauthorized insiders may have access to auxiliary datasets or contextual information enabling linkage, and the genomic data is retained in sufficient fidelity for matching.
uncertainty_note: This is a strong privacy concern for genomic raw data generally, though the exact PANOPTIC fit depends on whether the system treats the data as de-identified before storage.

title: Compute-node profiling from raw sequence data
description: Sending raw sequence data from the cluster filesystem to compute nodes enables the compute environment to assemble and organize detailed data points about specific data subjects from this single source in order to derive objective-specific outputs. Because genomic/sequence data is highly individualizing, this flow can support creation of per-subject profiles even if profiling is not the primary business purpose.
assumptions: The sequence data relates to identifiable or reasonably linkable individuals, and compute jobs can access enough record-level content or metadata to organize subject-level characteristics.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC retrieval suggests profiling, but the exact sub-activity fit depends on whether the compute stage actually structures results per individual rather than performing only aggregate/stateless transformation.

title: Compute nodes can distinguish and target individuals within sequence datasets
description: Once raw sequence data is delivered to compute nodes, the processing environment may distinguish particular data subjects or subsets for differentiated treatment, such as selective analysis, prioritization, filtering, or downstream handling. This constitutes targeting when the flow enables singling out specific subjects for special processing.
assumptions: Jobs or operators can isolate records, samples, or subject-linked sequence entries and apply different logic or handling to them.
uncertainty_note: Targeting is plausible for per-sample analytical workflows, but may not apply if all records are processed uniformly with no subject-specific selection.

title: Research data is made available in the delivery DMZ beyond its necessary lifecycle or audience
description: Sending context-relevant research data from the cluster filesystem into the data delivery DMZ creates a disclosure risk if the DMZ makes the dataset available after the legitimate delivery window, or to a broader set of recipients than required. PANOPTIC PA10.01 applies because the flow explicitly prepares data for availability/distribution, which can afford revelations if retention, access scope, or publication controls are not tightly constrained.
assumptions: The DMZ is a staging area for downstream delivery and may be reachable by parties or systems with broader access than the source store. The data may still contain direct or indirect identifiers or otherwise sensitive research content.

title: Transfer to the delivery DMZ increases linkability of research data across delivery contexts
description: Once the generated research data is staged in the data delivery DMZ, the same dataset may become observable, correlatable, or reusable across multiple delivery events, recipients, or access logs. This can enable linkability between records, requests, projects, or recipients that were more isolated in the source filesystem. The disclosure-enabling nature of PA10.01 is relevant because making data available in a delivery-facing store can expose stable identifiers, metadata, filenames, timestamps, or dataset structure that support correlation.
assumptions: The DMZ preserves metadata, filenames, transfer logs, or stable dataset handles that can be correlated across deliveries or with external knowledge.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the DMZ exposing or retaining correlatable metadata; if the delivery store strips such metadata and enforces one-time isolated delivery, applicability is reduced.

title: Delivery staging may enable re-identification of data previously treated as de-identified
description: Moving research data into the data delivery DMZ can enable re-identification if the staged package includes quasi-identifiers, richer metadata, multiple extracts, or delivery-side joins that re-associate previously de-identified data with individuals. PA05.01.01 applies where the act of preparing and exposing data for delivery creates conditions for re-association.
assumptions: The research data may be pseudonymised or de-identified rather than fully anonymous, and the delivery environment or recipients may have access to auxiliary information.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether the dataset is de-identified; this threat is most applicable when the 'context-relevant research data' has undergone de-identification or pseudonymisation prior to transfer.

title: Sample release request may bypass regulatory or policy constraints
description: The DNA Store receives a physical sample request from an external researcher for release of a biological specimen. If the store fulfills the request without validating consent scope, ethics approval, chain-of-custody requirements, permitted use, or applicable legal restrictions, the disclosure and transfer of the specimen can violate regulatory or organizational privacy obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the requested sample is linked to or derived from an identifiable or potentially identifiable person and that release decisions are made or actioned at the DNA Store.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match PA13.04 is strong for non-compliant release, but the exact LINDDUN tree node is best-effort because PANOPTIC rather than DFD-position methodology is being used.

title: Sample release may pre-empt the data subject's privacy choices
description: Processing a physical sample request and dispatching the specimen to a sequencing lab could occur before the data subject has an opportunity to exercise relevant privacy controls, such as withdrawal, restriction, or objections to secondary use. This undermines the individual's ability to influence downstream handling of their biological material.
assumptions: Assumes the specimen is subject to participant preferences, dynamic consent, or withdrawal rights that should be checked before release.
uncertainty_note: PA07.09 is applicable if participant choices can affect release; if no such controls exist in scope, this threat may not apply.

title: Disclosing a biological sample to a new recipient exposes highly sensitive personal material
description: Fulfilling the request causes the DNA Store to transfer a biological sample to another party for sequencing. Biological specimens inherently carry sensitive personal and potentially genetic information, so release to an external recipient increases the risk of privacy-impacting disclosure beyond the original holding context.
assumptions: Assumes the sequencing lab is a separate recipient context from the store and that the sample remains attributable or linkable to an individual at least within the processing ecosystem.
uncertainty_note: PA03.11 is directly about biological samples, but the flow is a request rather than the actual sample transfer; this threat is grounded in the release decision triggered by this request, so applicability is indirect but still plausible.

title: Researcher obtains an identifiable biological specimen from storage
description: The flow delivers a physical biological sample from the DNA Store to the NCCoE Researcher. A biological specimen inherently contains rich personal and genetic information, so releasing it to a recipient creates a privacy threat of disclosure of highly sensitive data to that recipient, especially if access is broader than necessary or insufficiently authorized.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample remains linkable to an individual directly or through accompanying request/reference information, and that the researcher can access or further analyze the specimen.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 is defined around collecting biological samples from the data subject, while this flow is retrieval from storage rather than initial collection. I use it as the closest PANOPTIC grounding because the privacy risk arises from handling/transferring a biological sample.

title: Retrieved biological sample enables linkage to a specific data subject
description: By retrieving the physical sample referenced by a request, the researcher may be able to associate the specimen with a particular person or correlate it with other records, enabling linkage of the individual across datasets or contexts. The specimen itself can act as a strong identifier when combined with request metadata or later genetic analysis.
assumptions: Assumes the sample container, request, chain-of-custody data, or downstream analysis provides identifiers or quasi-identifiers that permit association with a person.
uncertainty_note: Linkability depends on what identifiers accompany the sample or are available to the researcher; the flow description does not specify these details.

title: Research use of stored specimen may exceed the data subject's expectations or consent
description: Retrieving a stored physical sample for researcher use can create a privacy threat if the specimen is used for purposes, analyses, or retention beyond what the data subject expected or authorized. Biological samples can support new inferences and secondary uses that are difficult for the subject to anticipate or control.
assumptions: Assumes consent, notice, or governance constraints may limit who can retrieve the sample or for what purposes it can be used.
uncertainty_note: This threat is grounded more in downstream use after retrieval than in the transfer alone, but the retrieval flow is the enabling step for such detectability/disclosure risks around biological samples.

title: Collection of a biological sample reveals highly sensitive personal data
description: The receiving clerk's acceptance of the physical sample initiates collection of biological material that can expose uniquely identifying and health-related information about the researcher/data subject. Even before sequencing, possession of the specimen creates a privacy threat because the sample inherently contains sensitive personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is derived from or directly associated with an identifiable or identifiable-by-context individual, as implied by a research sample sent for sequencing.

title: Biological sample enables strong linkability across research and laboratory contexts
description: A biological specimen can act as a persistent identifier and may allow records from the NCCoE researcher, sequencing lab, and downstream datasets to be linked together. The act of receiving the sample therefore creates a linkability threat across contexts and processing stages.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is labeled, accompanied by metadata, or intrinsically distinctive enough to support linkage with other records or datasets.

title: Sample collection or intake may exceed the intended scope of collection
description: This transfer may create a detectability/privacy issue if the laboratory intake collects or accepts a biological sample, accompanying materials, or identifying context beyond what is necessary for the stated sequencing purpose. Over-collection increases exposure and can make the subject more readily detectable within the processing environment.
assumptions: Assumes intake procedures may include extra specimen quantity, redundant identifiers, or ancillary paperwork beyond what is required for the research objective.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match for PA06.09 is similarity-retrieved and may be approximate for this flow; included because scope creep at collection/intake is a plausible threat, not because explicit evidence of over-collection was provided.

title: Collection of a biological sample exposes sensitive health/genetic data
description: The sample request form initiates collection of a biological specimen from the patient. Even at this handoff stage, the requested specimen inherently concerns highly sensitive health and potentially genetic information, creating a privacy threat because the patient is being asked to provide material from which intimate personal attributes may be derived.
assumptions: The requested physical sample is collected from the patient and later used for sequencing or related analysis.

title: Patient may be unaware of the scope of derived information from the requested sample
description: By receiving the test request form and proceeding to provide a biological sample, the patient may disclose far more information than is apparent from the immediate clinical request. Biological specimens can enable inference of genetic, familial, and health-related information beyond the apparent purpose of collection.
assumptions: The request form or surrounding process may not fully explain downstream analytical potential and secondary implications of sequencing-related specimen collection.
uncertainty_note: This depends on how clearly the clinician and form explain what can be derived from the sample.

title: Sample request can create linkability between patient identity and future specimen/results
description: Providing the patient with a request form for a physical sample establishes or reinforces a linkage between the patient's identity and the specimen to be collected, enabling later association of the biological sample and sequencing outputs with the identified patient across collection and laboratory contexts.
assumptions: The form carries identifiers or other metadata that travel with the sample or are used to match the sample to the patient.

title: Clinician collection of biological sample beyond patient expectation or necessity
description: When the clinician retrieves the patient's physical sample, they are handling and effectively collecting a biological specimen for use in care or related processing. This creates a privacy threat if the sample is obtained, retained, or used without sufficient necessity, transparency, or scope limitation, because the specimen can reveal highly sensitive health and genetic information about the patient.
assumptions: The flow represents transfer of custody or access to a patient-linked specimen from the patient side to the clinician, and the specimen is identifiable or reasonably linkable to the patient.
uncertainty_note: PA03.11 is a strong fit because the flow concerns a physical biological sample, but the wording 'retrieves the physical sample referenced by the physical sample request' may indicate custody transfer rather than initial collection from the body.

title: Excessive sensitivity exposure through clinician access to biological specimen
description: A biological sample inherently exposes more information than may be needed for the immediate purpose, including possible future inferences about health status, identity, or genetics. By retrieving the sample, the clinician gains access to a highly information-dense artifact, creating a risk of disproportionate data disclosure relative to the stated purpose.
assumptions: The sample contains analyzable biological material and is associated with the patient in a way that permits clinical or administrative use.
uncertainty_note: Mapped to disclosure of information because biological samples are rich in sensitive information, though some LINDDUN analyses might classify this primarily as detectability/content unawareness depending on system context.

title: Patient linkability through specimen retrieval and handling
description: Retrieval and handling of the physical sample may enable linkage between the specimen, the patient's identity, and other records or requests. Even if the sample were pseudonymized, operational handling by the clinician can re-establish or strengthen the link between specimen and patient, increasing privacy risk.
assumptions: The sample request or accompanying workflow includes identifiers, labels, or contextual metadata that allow the clinician to associate the specimen with the patient.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on whether the specimen and request are directly identified or can be linked in practice during retrieval.

title: Collection of biological sample enables identification through inherently identifying biomaterial
description: The receiving clerk's intake of the physical specimen constitutes collection of a biological sample. Even before sequencing, the specimen may contain direct or inferable identifiers and can later be linked to the resulting research data and the donor, creating an identifiability risk for the data subject.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is traceable to a patient/participant through labels, chain-of-custody data, or later laboratory linkage.

title: Physical specimen collection and transfer disclose highly sensitive personal data
description: Receiving and handling the biological sample exposes highly sensitive health/genetic material. The transfer itself increases the risk that intimate information about the data subject is disclosed beyond what is necessary, especially if packaging, labeling, or handling practices reveal identity or clinical context.
assumptions: Assumes the specimen or accompanying handling context can reveal health, genetic, or clinical information to lab staff or others with access.

title: Sample intake may exceed consent or collection scope
description: The sequencing lab's receipt of the physical sample may be out of scope if the collection, transfer, or intended downstream research use exceeds the limits established by consent, protocol, policy, or law. This creates a non-compliance risk tied specifically to the act of accepting the sample for sequencing.
assumptions: Assumes scope limits exist (e.g., consent restricted to clinical care, limited research purposes, or specific analyses) and that the receiving clerk's intake operationalizes the collection for sequencing.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the actual consent/protocol boundaries; the retrieved PANOPTIC context supports this pattern generally, but the concrete scope violation is not evidenced in the flow description alone.

title: Receipt of biological sample supports linkability across clinical and research contexts
description: When the receiving clerk accepts the specimen, the sample and its identifiers can act as a bridge between the clinician's context and the sequencing lab's research context. This enables records and derived data to be linked across systems, purposes, or episodes involving the same person.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is labeled or accompanied by metadata enabling later matching to clinical records or research outputs.

title: Request for digital sample data enables disclosure of recorded digital artifacts
description: This flow requests retrieval of digital sample data from the Digital Sample Data Store for onward transfer to a sequencing lab. If the stored digital sample includes recorded digital artifacts representing an aspect or likeness of a person, the request and release of that record creates a privacy threat of disclosure because personal data may be exposed beyond the original collection context.
assumptions: Assumes the 'digital sample data' contains personal or person-linked recorded artifacts rather than fully anonymous technical metadata only.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 (Recording) is the closest retrieved PANOPTIC activity for digital sample artifacts, but the flow is a retrieval/request rather than original collection, so this mapping is best-effort.

title: Requested digital sample data may permit re-identification
description: Providing digital sample data from the store in response to this request may allow the recipient or downstream sequencing lab to re-associate previously de-identified or pseudonymized sample data with a specific individual. This creates an identifiability threat if the dataset contains quasi-identifiers, sample identifiers, or can be linked with other records.
assumptions: Assumes the stored digital sample data is not fully anonymous and that auxiliary data exists to support linkage.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly say the data is de-identified, so the re-identification risk depends on dataset content and surrounding controls.

title: Cross-context linkage of digital sample data to researcher or lab-held records
description: The requested transfer of digital sample data from the store for use by the sequencing lab can enable linkage between the stored sample record and other datasets held by researchers or the lab. Such linking can reveal that multiple records concern the same data subject, increasing privacy exposure even if direct identifiers are absent.
assumptions: Assumes shared identifiers, stable specimen metadata, or other linkable attributes exist across systems.
uncertainty_note: Linked-identifiability is a plausible consequence of releasing digital sample data, but the exact linkage mechanism is not specified in the flow description.

title: Researcher access to digital sample data may exceed necessity
description: When the NCCoE Researcher retrieves digital sample data from the Digital Sample Data Store, the transfer can expose sensitive artifacts representing a data subject beyond what is necessary for the specific research task or request. Digital sample data is analogous to PANOPTIC Recording when it consists of captured digital artifacts about a person; unnecessary or overly broad retrieval increases the privacy risk of disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data contains personal or person-linked digital artifacts and that the requester may receive more detail, records, or fidelity than is strictly needed for the approved purpose.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 (Recording) is the closest retrieved PANOPTIC sub-activity for 'digital sample data', but this mapping is approximate because the flow concerns retrieval/access rather than initial collection.

title: Retrieved sample data may enable identification of the data subject
description: The digital sample data delivered to the NCCoE Researcher may contain sufficient direct or indirect attributes for the researcher to identify, or re-identify, the data subject. Even if the request references a sample rather than a named individual, combining the retrieved artifact with other accessible information can reveal identity.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data includes unique, quasi-identifying, or high-dimensional features and that the researcher has access to auxiliary information.
uncertainty_note: PA05.01 is a plausible fit where identity is inferred from retrieved sample data, but the exact identification pathway is not specified in the flow description.

title: Sample retrieval can make the subject linkable across requests or datasets
description: Providing the same or sufficiently distinctive digital sample data to the NCCoE Researcher can allow records about the same data subject to be linked across multiple requests, projects, or external datasets. Distinctive digital artifacts often act as stable correlators even when explicit identifiers are absent.
assumptions: Assumes repeated retrievals, persistent sample identifiers, or distinctive content/features that can be matched across contexts.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC context retrieved does not include a stronger direct 'linking' activity; using PA05.01 here because identification from combined data commonly also enables linkability. Tree node selection is best-effort.

title: Lab technician receives an identifiable biological sample
description: The physical transfer of a biological specimen to the lab technician exposes highly sensitive personal data inherent in the sample itself. Because biological samples can reveal health, genetic, or other intimate characteristics, the receiving party may learn more about the data subject than is necessary for the specific research task if the specimen is not minimized or properly separated from identity/context.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is linked, directly or indirectly, to an identifiable participant or project context and is not fully anonymized before handoff.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 explicitly fits biological sample handling, but mapping this transfer step to a LINDDUN disclosure node is best-effort because the flow is a handoff rather than initial collection.

title: Biological specimen can enable linkage across research contexts
description: A biological sample sent to the lab technician may carry identifiers or quasi-identifiers that permit linkage to other datasets, prior samples, or study records. Even where explicit identifiers are removed, specimen characteristics, labels, accession numbers, or project metadata accompanying the sample may allow the technician to correlate the specimen with a particular participant or cohort.
assumptions: Assumes labels, chain-of-custody metadata, or specimen characteristics are sufficient to correlate the sample with other records or contexts.
uncertainty_note: Linkability depends heavily on surrounding metadata and handling practices; the flow description alone does not confirm what identifiers accompany the specimen.

title: Sample transfer may exceed approved collection/use scope for the research project
description: Sending the physical sample to a lab technician working on a relevant project may still constitute a privacy threat if the transfer goes beyond the scope originally authorized for collection or handling. For example, the sample may be shared with a technician, lab function, or downstream analysis not covered by participant consent, protocol limitations, or other governing constraints.
assumptions: Assumes there are purpose, consent, protocol, or role-based limits on who may receive or analyze the sample.
uncertainty_note: Using PA06.09 here is a best-effort fit: the retrieved PANOPTIC item is phrased as collection out of scope, while this flow is a transfer/use step that may still operationalize an out-of-scope handling risk.

title: Physical sample handoff may not be adequately logged or detectable
description: If the transfer of the sample from the receiving clerk to the lab technician is not reliably recorded, the organization may be unable to demonstrate who handled the specimen, when it was transferred, or whether it was accessed inappropriately. This undermines accountability for privacy-relevant processing of the sample and hampers investigation of misuse or unauthorized handling.
assumptions: Assumes chain-of-custody or transfer-event logging is required for accountable sample handling and may be incomplete for this physical handoff.
uncertainty_note: PA04.04 concerns detection failure rather than the transfer itself; it is included because physical handoffs commonly create accountability gaps, but the flow description does not explicitly mention logging controls.

title: Collection of biological specimen by wet lab creates exposure of highly sensitive personal data
description: Receiving the physical sample at the wet lab constitutes collection/handling of a biological specimen. Biological samples inherently contain rich, sensitive personal data (e.g., genetic and health-related information), so this flow creates a privacy threat if the lab collects or accepts the sample beyond what is necessary, without adequate justification, or without the data subject's informed expectations being met.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is directly or indirectly linkable to an identifiable person and is intended for sequencing or related analysis.

title: Wet lab receipt of the sample may enable processing beyond the subject's awareness
description: Transferring the physical sample to the wet lab can reduce the data subject's visibility into where the specimen is held, what analyses are performed, and how long the specimen is retained. Because biological samples can support additional present or future analyses beyond the immediate sequencing purpose, this handoff creates a risk that processing or retention occurs without sufficient awareness or transparency to the data subject.
assumptions: Assumes the subject is not continuously informed about downstream laboratory handling, secondary analysis, or retention practices for the specimen.
uncertainty_note: Grounded in PANOPTIC PA03.11 Biological sample; transparency aspects are inferred from the handoff context rather than explicitly stated in the flow description.

title: Biological sample transfer enables strong linkability to the data subject
description: A biological specimen is a powerful identifier and can often be linked back to a specific individual, especially when accompanied by operational metadata or laboratory accessioning. Sending the sample to the wet lab therefore creates a linkability threat if the specimen, labels, or associated records allow the lab or others to connect the sample with the data subject across datasets, episodes, or systems.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is labeled, accessioned, or otherwise associated with identifying or quasi-identifying metadata during receipt by the wet lab.

title: Patient cannot practically manage or transform the delivered results copy
description: The flow explicitly includes giving the patient a copy of interpreted clinical results. If that copy is provided only in a constrained format or through channels that prevent editing, correction, extraction, or onward portability, the patient may be unable to manage the information content about themselves in a meaningful way.
assumptions: Assumes the provided copy may be locked, non-portable, or otherwise difficult for the patient to modify, annotate, or transfer for second opinions or personal recordkeeping.
uncertainty_note: This is a plausible manageability threat grounded in the flow wording ('copy of the results'), but the DFD does not specify format or technical controls, so applicability is conditional.

title: Patient lacks control over onward disclosure of interpreted results
description: When the counselor provides interpreted results and recommendations, the patient may not have effective control over how those results are subsequently shared by the custodian ecosystem, especially if distribution to other care participants, family-related workflows, or affiliated providers is preconfigured or poorly governed.
assumptions: Assumes this counseling interaction is part of a broader clinical workflow where results may be shared beyond this conversation and the patient has limited ability to set or enforce disclosure preferences.
uncertainty_note: The threat is relevant to the sensitivity of genetic results, but this specific flow only shows disclosure from counselor to patient; limited evidence in the DFD for the onward-sharing mechanism.

title: Exposure of sensitive genetic results during counselor-to-patient communication
description: Interpreted clinical results and recommendations are highly sensitive health and genetic data. If this flow occurs through an insecure channel, in a non-private setting, or with inadequate identity verification, the information could become accessible to unintended parties, resulting in exposure.
assumptions: Assumes the meeting or delivery channel could be observable by others (e.g., email, portal misdelivery, shared device, overheard telehealth/in-person session).

title: Interception of clinical genetic results in transit to the patient
description: The flow sends interpreted clinical genetic results and professional recommendations from the Genetic Physician to the Patient. If the communication channel is insecure or accessible to unintended parties, an attacker or bystander could intercept highly sensitive health/genetic information during transmission.
assumptions: Assumes results may be communicated over channels such as email, portal messaging, phone, printed mail, or other media that could be observed or captured if not adequately protected.
uncertainty_note: PA03.07 is a strong fit for in-transit compromise, but the exact communication medium for this flow is not specified.

title: Patient lacks control over onward disclosure of communicated results
description: Once interpreted results and recommendations are delivered, the patient may have limited ability to control how the information is further shared by the sender's chosen communication mechanism or by involved intermediaries. This can reduce the individual's control over disclosure of sensitive genetic information.
assumptions: Assumes the delivery mechanism or surrounding workflow may expose the information to intermediaries, shared devices/accounts, or other recipients beyond the patient's intended audience.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the actual delivery channel and workflow. PA07.04 is relevant if the patient cannot meaningfully choose or constrain how disclosure occurs.

title: Manipulative secondary use of research data in clinical report generation
description: The Clinical Result Generation App receives context-relevant research data and uses it to create a final clinical report. If the app leverages research-context data to influence, steer, or inappropriately shape outcomes delivered about the data subject beyond the expected clinical purpose, this is a privacy threat grounded in PANOPTIC PA11.03 Manipulation. The risk is that data originally held in the cluster filesystem for research context could be used to exploit or unfairly affect the subject through the report content or downstream decisions.
assumptions: Assumes the research data may include sensitive or inferential attributes not strictly necessary for the final clinical reporting purpose, and that use-governance or purpose-limitation controls may be weak or absent.
uncertainty_note: Moderate confidence. PA11.03 is the strongest retrieved PANOPTIC match, but the exact threat depends on whether the research data is used beyond the subject's reasonable expectations or intended purpose.

title: Bypass of privacy controls on research-data use during report generation
description: This flow may enable the Clinical Result Generation App to consume context-relevant research data from the cluster filesystem while ignoring or defeating privacy controls such as consent restrictions, role-based access boundaries, or purpose/use constraints. Under PANOPTIC PA07.08 Bypass of user controls, the privacy threat is that the app processes data for report generation despite controls meant to limit such use.
assumptions: Assumes user or organizational privacy controls exist for the research dataset and are expected to constrain transfer or use in the clinical-reporting context.
uncertainty_note: Moderate confidence. The flow alone does not prove control bypass; the threat applies if report generation can proceed without enforcing applicable privacy preferences or governance controls.

title: Third party re-identifies the patient across prior study records
description: The receiving 3rd Party Previous Enrollment Entity updates its records for studies involving the patient by linking newly provided genetic-counseling results to an existing or previously de-identified/pseudonymized enrollment record. This creates a privacy threat when identity is re-associated with records that had been separated from direct identity, enabling the party to know which study records belong to the patient.
assumptions: Applies if the receiving entity's study/enrollment records are de-identified, coded, pseudonymized, or otherwise not currently directly linked to the patient's identity, and the update request restores that association.
uncertainty_note: The flow explicitly says 'Patient Re-identification Request,' so PA05.01.01 is strongly indicated. The exact LINDDUN tree-node mapping is best-effort because PANOPTIC, not classic DFD-position analysis, is primary here.

title: Linkability created by merging counseling results with prior enrollment records
